title: What protects Japan's economy? And what does it mean for the yen?
body: What protects Japan's economy? And what does it mean for the yen? Japan has global businesses, valuable overseas investments and a central bank moving away from years of very low interest rates. But a strong economy does not automatically mean a strong currency. Look at a Japanese castle surrounded by a moat and a simple idea comes to mind: the water and walls help protect what is inside. An economy can have defenses too. Japan's include businesses that sell products around the world and substantial investments in other countries. But its defenses have gaps, including a reliance on imported energy. That raises an interesting question for anyone watching the Japanese yen: if Japan has so many economic strengths, why can its currency still struggle against the US dollar? The answer begins with a distinction. The strength of an economy and the price of its currency are connected, but they do not always move together. Japan's economic moat Japan is home to companies known around the world for cars, machinery, electronics and other products. It also supplies materials and equipment used to make computer chips. When people and businesses abroad buy Japanese products, that creates income for Japanese companies and supports jobs at home. Japan's exports of cars, semiconductors and chipmaking equipment grew in September, according to trade figures reported by The Japan Times. Japan also owns substantial investments overseas.

body: Taken at face value, a thaw in US-Canada trade relations would support the Canadian dollar and trade-exposed Canadian equities, which have carried the cost of months of tit-for-tat tariffs. Markets are likely to discount the headline until there is text to read, though, because neither side has said what tariffs would change or when. The timing, two days before midterms in which tariffs on Canada are a live issue in some border states, also invites scepticism over how much is policy and how much is campaign messaging. Any detail from the negotiating teams in the coming weeks will matter far more to the loonie than Sunday's remarks. -- Washington and Ottawa are now very close to a deal in concept, which is reassuring for anyone who trades concepts, while everyone else waits for something with tariff rates in it.

title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Monday, November 2, 2026 - another China PMI
body: China's private-sector manufacturing PMI is due at 01:45 GMT on Monday (20:45 US Eastern on Sunday), with economists expecting factory activity to keep growing in October, though at a slower pace than in September. The RatingDog China General Manufacturing PMI, compiled by S&P Global, is forecast to ease to 51.6 from 52.1, according to a Reuters poll. That would still leave the index comfortably above the 50 mark that separates expansion from contraction. September's reading beat expectations and was the strongest in five months, supported by firmer demand at home and abroad, with foreign sales growing at their fastest pace in seven months. The release follows a weak set of official figures on Saturday. The National Bureau of Statistics manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3 from 50.1, well below the 50.0 expected in the same Reuters poll, and new export orders dropped to 48.7. Statisticians attributed much of the decline to seasonal factors, including a pullback in overseas orders after a strong September. The two surveys often diverge. The RatingDog index samples a smaller group of around 650 firms with a heavier tilt toward export-oriented manufacturers, and it collects responses in the second half of each month. The official survey covers more than 3,000 companies at month-end. The private gauge has typically produced the brighter of the two readings, and that gap was clear in September.

title: China's central bank, regulators to meet on stock support after record 12-week slide
body: Monday's session in mainland China and Hong Kong is the first chance for equities to react to the reports, and the prospect of state-backed support may help sentiment at the open after October's heavy selling. Whether that lasts is likely to depend on detail. Traders have already seen last month's measures fail to halt the slide, so the scale and terms of any expanded relending facility will matter more than the signal alone. A credible support package could also ease some pressure on the yuan and on broader Asian risk appetite. Without concrete steps, the combination of contracting PMIs and doubts over AI earnings leaves the downside case in place. --- After a record losing streak in Chinese stocks, Beijing appears to be reaching for more support tools, though last month showed that a signal on its own is not enough. Info via Bloomberg (gated).

title: OPEC+ holds December targets steady for third month as Hormuz disruption persists
body: The rollover was widely expected and does little to change near-term supply, because most of the producers involved cannot reach their existing targets while Hormuz flows remain disrupted. That leaves physical availability tied to the waterway rather than to OPEC+ policy, a point reinforced by Iran's claim on Sunday that two tankers hit mines and exploded there. For oil traders, the near-term risk is still skewed toward supply disruption. The medium-term counterweight is the surplus forecasters see if Gulf barrels return in 2027, which puts the November 29 quota decision at the centre of next year's supply outlook. --- OPEC+ chose to wait rather than act, keeping December targets flat because the Iran war, not quota policy, is setting how much Gulf oil actually reaches the market.

title: China's factory and services PMI gauges both drop below 50 as fourth quarter starts on a weak note
body: Because the data came out on a Saturday, Monday's Asian session is the first chance for markets to price the miss. Softer Chinese factory demand is usually a headwind for industrial metals such as copper and iron ore, and for China-sensitive currencies including the yuan and the Australian dollar. Chinese equities may be partly cushioned by expectations of more policy support. For oil, a weaker demand signal from a key crude buyer would normally weigh on prices, but for now it is likely to be overshadowed by supply risk in the Strait of Hormuz. Price sub-indices that are easing but still elevated also weaken the case for reading the release as disinflationary. --- Earlier ICYMI: Morgan Stanley sees 10%-15% more downside for Chinese offshore stocks before a bottom --- China's brief return to factory growth lasted a month, with October's PMIs slipping below 50 across the board and putting Beijing's stimulus intentions back in the spotlight.

title: Iran says two tankers hit mines in Hormuz as Tehran offers two-day reopening plan
body: A claim that mines are now disabling tankers in Hormuz, including a supertanker, raises the perceived physical risk of every transit, not just those Iran targets, and is likely to feed through to freight rates, war-risk insurance premiums and the geopolitical premium in crude. The reopening plan offers a theoretical path to restored flows, but its conditions reach well beyond shipping, so traders are likely to treat it as a negotiating position rather than a near-term supply fix. Until there is independent confirmation of the incident and a US response to the proposal, upside risk to oil looks more immediate than the prospect of relief. - Iran is using both mines and mediation in Hormuz, claiming two tankers were blown up on an unapproved route while offering to reopen the strait in two days, if Washington meets a demanding price.
